name: AE-FishBIT
summary: Miniaturised tool called AEFishBIT has been designed to monitor individual farmed fish in a non-invasive manner. Weighing less than one gram, AEFishBIT is a tiny programmable & reconfigurable tri-axial accelerometer for data recording and processing. The prototype is externally attached to the fish operculum to monitor physical activity by mapping accelerations in x- and y-axes, while operculum beats (z-axis) serve as a measurement of respiratory frequency. The device has been tested and validated in gilthead sea bream and European sea bass. Preliminary works with cultured salmon also show promising results. Visual observations regarding tissue damage, feeding behaviour and circulating levels of stress markers did not suggest a negative impact from device tagging. To the best of the researchers’ knowledge there is currently no other tagging device that provides a simultaneous measurement of both physical activity and respiratory frequency in a non-invasive manner. Field tests with free-swimming fish facing a wide array of biotic and abiotic factors have highlighted the association of AEFishBIT measurements with better performance or differences in stress and disease resilience

Typically, a landlord includes the cost of utilities in the rent. In the calculations, the average values of total consumption, divided between tenants, depending on the rented area, are used. summary: The Bromalgae project is summarized as a disruptive and innovative technology, rarely seen in the industry. Bromalgae has developed liquid trees, which contain living microalgae inside. These microorganisms have a carbon assimilation capacity 25 times greater than terrestrial trees. Microalgae are responsible for 75% of global CO2 fixation. They are found in both freshwater (reservoirs, lakes, rivers) and saltwater. Ecologically, they are classified as phytoplankton and are responsible for oxygenating the atmosphere, providing 50% of the oxygen we breathe. The GarbiAir system is installed in urban areas with the highest emissions, such as zones with heavy vehicular traffic. A blower captures the surrounding air, which passes through pre-filters to remove suspended particles and harmful microorganisms that could affect the microalgae. The photobioreactor is fed with the CO2 and NOx from this air, which enters the system through bubbling, aiding in the system's agitation process, along with other essential nutrients in the medium and light. This process enables photosynthesis. Using sensors, the concentrations of CO2 and NOx are continuously monitored. Two sensors are placed at the photobioreactor's entrance and exit to observe the difference in concentration. Depending on the weather conditions, the light intensity can be adjusted to optimize the photosynthetic process and prevent oxidative stress in the microalgal cells. First GarbiAir pilot plant in Barakaldo (Bizkaia) In June 2023, we inaugurated our first liquid microalgae vegetation system, GarbiAir, in Barakaldo. The idea is simple: KorallionBio‘s cascade approach focuses on maximizing the value from a production process by using every part of the materials involved. It starts with creating an initial product, where anything not used is typically considered waste. In the next step, this leftover material is further processed to extract any remaining useful products or ingredients. At this point, KorallionBio steps in using microalgae, which convert the remaining nutrients and molecules in this waste into high-value biomolecules. name: ReefSystems
summary: MOSES (Modular Sealife System) is a modular artificial reef technology developed by ReefSystems in the Netherlands to enhance marine biodiversity and restore degraded aquatic ecosystems. It consists of interlocking reef units that can be assembled into reef structures and placed in oceans, coastal waters, estuaries, canals, or around marine infrastructure. Once installed, the modules create complex habitats with varied surfaces, cavities and microhabitats where marine life — such as oysters, mussels, seaweeds, fish and other organisms — can find food, shelter and space to reproduce. Key features: Nature-inclusive artificial reef: Designed to mimic natural hard substrates that attract and support a wide range of aquatic species. Modular and adaptable: Units can be configured to suit different seabed conditions, project goals and scales, from small installations in urban waterways to large coastal reef projects. Functional and multifunctional: Besides ecological uplift, MOSES reefs can be integrated with coastal or offshore structures (e.g., dikes, quay walls, floating solar anchoring systems) to add habitat value while fulfilling engineering functions. Climate-aware production: Made using materials and methods aimed at reducing CO₂ emissions compared to traditional concrete, with ecological monitoring in collaboration with scientific partners. MOSES has been deployed in multiple pilot and operational projects, including large installations along the Lauwersmeerdijk in the Wadden Sea, as well as experimental reefs in places like the Noordzeekanaal and Haringvliet, demonstrating measurable increases in species richness and ecosystem complexity. In short, MOSES turns engineered marine structures into thriving underwater ecosystems, bridging ecological restoration with practical infrastructure needs.

name: BlueRizon
summary: BlueRizon is a large-scale mangrove restoration programme located along the north coast of Java, Indonesia. The project targets 5,000 hectares of restoration within a selected area of approximately 6,430 hectares, spread across 35 districts in three provinces, West Java, Central Java and East Java, and engages up to 122 coastal villages. It combines Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation (ARR) with Wetland Restoration and Conservation (WRC) on degraded coastal parcels, abandoned or converted tambak ponds and riverbanks along the Pantura coastline. The project is being developed under Verra’s Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) v5.0 using methodology VM0033 v2.1, with Climate, Community & Biodiversity (CCB) certification pursued in parallel. The carbon crediting period is 40 years and a benefit-sharing with communities up to 70 years. Beyond carbon sequestration, BlueRizon aims to strengthen coastal protection, restore fishery ecosystem services and stabilize shorelines exposed to sea-level rise and erosion, while generating lasting socio-economic co-benefits for local communities, including nursery employment, transition to silvofishery, support for women-led economic activities such as batik and food processing, and enhanced climate resilience for partner villages.

The modular turbine is the only one worldwide which does not need a fixed rotation axis. Main advantages for yachts are its complete quietness, no need for superstructural parts and power generation on 24h per day (compared to solar cells) . After R&D, prototyping and finally 2 years of real life testing and optimization the wind turbine is ready for market. name: Zenco BlueStone
summary: Zenco's core innovation is the Zenethane™ feedstock pellet — a proprietary seaweed-blended formulation engineered with anaerobic digestion additives at the cultivation stage. Unlike conventional AD feedstocks, the pellet is pre-optimised for maximum biogas yield before it reaches the plant, eliminating pre-treatment costs and yield variability for operators. The pellet is produced during offshore seaweed cultivation, structured as a natural capital project: ocean bioremediation and CO₂ drawdown are the primary purpose; feedstock supply is the commercial consequence. The pellet drives three commercial outputs from a single process: Zenethane™ (certified biomethane, ISCC EU certifiable, GGCS-registered), Zenthilizer™ (premium bio-fertiliser from the high K, N and P content of seaweed digestate), and in Phase 2, Zenthynol™ (drop-in SAF, diesel and LPG via Fischer-Tropsch synthesis). The pellet is also licensable to third-party AD operators as a standalone recurring revenue stream.

name: Keep it fresh
summary: Fresh food, and seafood in particular, spoils fast. Fish and other catch are highly perishable: once landed they must move immediately through an energy-intensive cold chain, and even then a large share is downgraded or lost before it reaches the consumer. The European Union discards about 132 billion euros of food every year, and losses are among the highest in the most perishable categories such as fish, fruit and vegetables. The current answer, continuous refrigeration, is expensive, energy-hungry, carbon-intensive and often unavailable to small fishers, coastal producers and cooperatives. Chemical preservatives raise clean-label and regulatory concerns. The result is wasted catch, wasted energy, and producers forced to sell immediately into a glutted market at depressed prices. There is no widely available way to hold fresh food, without a cold chain and without chemicals, long enough to reach better markets.
